blocks.p: By this time they had come within sight of the town of Vanity, where Vanity Fair is held. When they saw how near they were, they talked over how they should pass through it, and some said one thing and some another. At last Mr. Great-heart said, “As you know, I have often guided pilgrims through this town. I am acquainted with a Mr. Mnason, a Cypriot by birth and an old disciple, at whose house we can lodge. [Acts 21:16] If you think it good, we’ll turn in there.”
“Agreed,” said old Honest. “Agreed,” said Christiana. “Agreed,” said Mr. Feeble-mind; and so they all said.

Now it was evening by the time they reached the edge of the town, but Mr. Great-heart knew the way to the old man’s house, and there they came. He called at the door, and the old man inside knew his voice the moment he heard it. He opened, and they all came in.
“How far have you come today?” said Mnason, their host.
“From the house of our friend Gaius,” they said.
“I promise you, that is a good stretch. You may well be weary. Sit down.” So they sat.
“Come now, what cheer, sirs?” said their guide. “I dare say you are welcome to my friend.”
“I do bid you welcome,” said Mr. Mnason, “and whatever you need, only say so, and we will do what we can to get it for you.”
“A little while ago,” said Honest, “our great need was shelter and good company, and now I hope we have both.”
“For shelter, you see what it is. For good company, that will show itself in the trial.”
“Well,” said Mr. Great-heart, “will you take the pilgrims up to their lodging?”
“I will,” said Mr. Mnason, and he showed them to their rooms, and also to a very fine dining room where they could sit and eat together until it was time to rest.
When they had taken their places and were a little cheered after their journey, Mr. Honest asked his landlord whether there was any store of good people in the town.
“We have a few,” said Mnason, “and indeed they are only a few, compared with those on the other side.”
“But how can we arrange to see some of them? To people on pilgrimage, the sight of good men is like the moon and the stars coming out to sailors at sea.”

Then Mr. Mnason stamped his foot, and his daughter Grace came up. “Grace,” he said, “go and tell my friends Mr. Contrite, Mr. Holy-man, Mr. Love-saint, Mr. Dare-not-lie, and Mr. Penitent that I have a friend or two at my house who would like to see them this evening.”
So Grace went to call them, and they came; and after greetings they all sat down together at the table.

“My neighbors,” said Mr. Mnason, “as you see, I have a company of strangers at my house. They are pilgrims; they come from far away, and they are going to Mount Zion. But who do you think this is?” And he pointed to Christiana. “This is Christiana, the wife of Christian, that famous pilgrim who, with his brother Faithful, was so shamefully treated in our town.”

At that they stood amazed. “We little thought to see Christiana when Grace came to call us,” they said. “What a welcome surprise this is.” Then they asked after her welfare, and whether these young men were her husband’s sons; and when she told them they were, they said, “May the King you love and serve make you like your father, and bring you where he is, in peace.”
When they were all seated, Mr. Honest asked Mr. Contrite and the others how matters stood in their town at present.

“You may be sure we are full of hurry in fair time,” said Mr. Contrite. “It is hard to keep our hearts and spirits in any good order when we are so hemmed in. A man who lives in a place like this, and has to deal with the people we deal with, needs a reminder every moment of the day to take heed.”
“But how are your neighbors for quietness?”

“They are far more moderate now than they used to be. You know how Christian and Faithful were treated in our town; but lately, as I say, they have been much more moderate. I think the blood of Faithful still lies heavy on them, for since they burned him they have been ashamed to burn anyone else. In those days we were afraid to walk the streets; now we can show our heads. Then the very name of a believer was hateful; now, in some parts of our town at least, for you know the town is large, religion is counted honorable.”
Then Mr. Contrite asked them, “And how does your pilgrimage go? How does the country stand toward you?”

“It goes with us as it goes with travelers,” said Honest. “Sometimes the road is clean and sometimes foul, sometimes uphill and sometimes down. We are seldom sure of anything. The wind is not always at our backs, and not everyone we meet on the road is a friend. We have met with some notable knocks already, and what is still ahead we do not know; but for the most part we find it true, as has been said of old, that a good man must suffer trouble.”
“You speak of knocks. What knocks have you met with?”
“Ask Mr. Great-heart, our guide. He can give the best account of that.”

“We have been set upon three or four times already,” said Great-heart. “First, Christiana and her children were attacked by two ruffians who, they feared, would have taken their lives. We were set upon by Giant Bloody-man, by Giant Maul, and by Giant Slay-good; though in truth we rather set upon the last than he on us. It happened like this. After we had been some time at the house of ‘Gaius, my host, and host of the whole church’ [Rom. 16:23], we decided one day to take our weapons and go see if we could find any of those who were enemies to pilgrims, for we had heard there was a notable one in the neighborhood. Gaius knew his haunt better than I did, since he lived nearby; so we searched and searched, until at last we made out the mouth of his cave. Then we were glad, and plucked up our spirits. We went up to his den, and when we got there, we found he had dragged this poor man, Mr. Feeble-mind, into his net by brute force and was about to make an end of him. But when he saw us, supposing, as we thought, that he had another prey, he left the poor man in his hole and came out. So we fell to it in earnest, and he laid about him lustily; but in the end he was brought to the ground and his head cut off and set up by the roadside, as a terror to any who should practice such wickedness after him. And that I am telling you the truth, here is the man himself to confirm it, who was like a lamb taken out of the lion’s mouth.”

“I found it true,” said Mr. Feeble-mind, “to my cost and to my comfort: to my cost, when he threatened every moment to pick my bones; and to my comfort, when I saw Mr. Great-heart and his friends coming so near with their weapons to deliver me.”

“There are two things that those who go on pilgrimage need to be possessed of,” said Mr. Holy-man: “courage, and an unspotted life. If they have no courage, they can never hold to their way; and if their lives are loose, they will make the very name of a pilgrim stink.”

“I hope that caution is not needed among you,” said Mr. Love-saint. “But truly, there are many on the road who show themselves strangers to pilgrimage rather than strangers and pilgrims on the earth.”

“It is true,” said Mr. Dare-not-lie. “They have neither the pilgrim’s bearing nor the pilgrim’s courage. They do not walk upright, but all askew; one shoe turns inward and the other out, their stockings hang down behind, a rag here and a tear there, to the disgrace of their Lord.”

“These are things they ought to be troubled about,” said Mr. Penitent, “and pilgrims are not likely to have the grace they desire put upon them and their progress until the road is cleared of such spots and blemishes.”
So they sat talking and passing the time until supper was set on the table; then they went to it and refreshed their weary bodies, and so to rest.
Now they stayed a great while at this fair, at the house of Mr. Mnason, who in time gave his daughter Grace to Christiana’s son Samuel as his wife, and his daughter Martha to Joseph.

The time they stayed here, as I said, was long, for it was not now as it had been in former days. So the pilgrims grew acquainted with many of the good people of the town and did them what service they could. Mercy, as was her habit, worked hard for the poor, so that their bellies and their backs blessed her, and she was an ornament to her faith there. And to tell the truth about Grace, Phoebe, and Martha, they were all of a very good nature and did much good in their place. All of them, too, had many children, so that Christian’s name, as was said before, was likely to live on in the world.

While they were here, a monster came out of the woods and killed many of the people of the town. It would also carry off their children and teach them to suck its whelps. No man in the town dared so much as face this monster; everyone fled at the sound of its coming.

The monster was like no beast on earth. Its body was like a dragon’s, and it had seven heads and ten horns. [Rev. 17:3] It made great havoc among the children, and yet it was governed by a woman. This monster laid down terms to men, and the men who loved their lives more than their souls accepted its terms. So they came under its power.

Now Mr. Great-heart, together with the men who had come to visit the pilgrims at Mr. Mnason’s house, made a covenant to go and engage this beast, in the hope of delivering the people of the town from the paws and jaws of so devouring a serpent.

So Mr. Great-heart, Mr. Contrite, Mr. Holy-man, Mr. Dare-not-lie, and Mr. Penitent went out with their weapons to meet it. At first the monster was very fierce and looked on these enemies with great disdain; but being sturdy men-at-arms, they gave it such a beating that they made it retreat, and they came home again to Mr. Mnason’s house.

The monster, you must know, had its particular seasons for coming out to make its attempts on the children of the town; and these brave worthies watched for it in those seasons and attacked it again and again, so that in time it became not only wounded but lame. It has not made the havoc among the townspeople’s children that it used to make, and some truly believe that the beast will die of its wounds.

This made Mr. Great-heart and his companions famous in the town, so that many of the people who had no taste for such things themselves still held them in reverence and respect. For this reason the pilgrims got little hurt here. True, there were some of the baser sort, who could see no further than a mole and understand no more than a beast; these had no reverence for the men and took no notice of their valor or their adventures.

Well, the time came on when the pilgrims had to go on their way, and they prepared for the journey. They sent for their friends and conferred with them, and they set some time apart to commit one another to the protection of their Prince. Again there were those who brought them what they had that was fit for the weak and the strong, for the women and the men, and loaded them with whatever they needed. [Acts 28:10]

Then they set out, their friends going with them as far as was convenient; and once more they committed one another to the protection of their King, and parted. The pilgrims’ company went on, with Mr. Great-heart in front. Since the women and children were weak, they had to go as fast as they could bear, and this gave Mr. Ready-to-stumble and Mr. Feeble-mind the more sympathy with their condition.

When they had left the townspeople, and their friends had said farewell, they soon came to the place where Faithful was put to death. There they stopped and gave thanks to the One who had enabled him to bear his cross so well, all the more because they now found that they had reaped a benefit from so manly a suffering as his.
After this they went on a good way, talking of Christian and Faithful, and of how Hopeful joined Christian after Faithful was dead.

Now they came up to the Hill Lucre, where the silver mine was that drew Demas away from his pilgrimage, and into which, as some think, Mr. Self-Interest fell and perished; and they thought about that. But when they came to the old monument that stood across from the Hill Lucre, the pillar of salt that stood within sight of Sodom and its stinking lake, they marveled, as Christian had before them, that men of such knowledge and ripe wit as those two were should have been so blind as to turn aside here. Only they considered again that human nature is not much affected by the harm that has come to others, especially when the thing in view has a power to draw the foolish eye.
